papers.title: VocalGrad: Evaluating Acoustic Perception in Audio Language Models
papers.abstract: Recent large audio language models (LALMs) have extended their capabilities beyond lexical speech understanding to tasks requiring paralinguistic and non-linguistic audio understanding, such as emotion recognition. However, these models still struggle to reliably utilize acoustic information, particularly when it co-occurs with spoken linguistic content. Existing benchmarks do not clearly distinguish acoustic perception from higher-level reasoning, making it difficult to identify the source of these failures. To address this issue, we introduce VocalGrad, a benchmark designed to evaluate LALMs'ability to perceive low-level acoustic variations. VocalGrad formulates this problem as a simple binary classification of temporal change direction, enabling evaluation largely independent of higher-level reasoning or semantic understanding. Our benchmark results reveal a substantial gap in acoustic perception between human annotators and state-of-the-art LALMs: while human annotators achieve high accuracy, LALMs perform at near-chance levels. We further conduct linear probing to identify structural bottlenecks in these models. Our analysis reveals two distinct failure modes: for some categories, task-relevant information is preserved in internal representations but not utilized by the language model head; for others, the information becomes progressively less linearly decodable across model layers. Overall, our results reveal substantial limitations of LALMs in modeling acoustic variation under controlled settings and expose representation differences not observable from text outputs.

papers.title: Too Emotional to Be Fake? Intra-Utterance Emotion Shifts Expose Failure Modes in Speech Deepfake Detectors
papers.abstract: Expressive speech synthesis can now change emotion within a single utterance, yet its impact on deepfake detection remains unclear. We introduce EmoShift, a benchmark comparing emotion-stable (AA) and emotion-changing (AB) speech to examine these effects while accounting for static emotion identity and acoustic confounds. It comprises 7,240 bona fide utterances from four source datasets and 9,720 synthetic utterances generated using four expressive TTS systems. Across seven detectors, we find that emotion changes can make synthetic speech appear more genuine, increasing spoof miss rates by up to 25.3 percentage points on OMG-Emotion at fixed thresholds. Conversely, emotion-changing bona fide speech increases false-alarm rates by up to 24.4 percentage points on IEMOCAP. Further analyses reveal detector-specific sensitivities to emotion trajectories, not fully explained by static emotion identity or splicing artifacts. These findings underscore the importance of emotion dynamics in deepfake detection.

papers.title: Development of a multilingual speech-to-text translation model to support artisans’ business communication
papers.abstract: Effective communication between artisans and customers remains difficult in multilingual commercial settings in which English interacts with indigenous and contact languages such as Yoruba and Nigerian Pidgin. This study developed and evaluated a lightweight English-to-Yoruba and English-to-Nigerian Pidgin speech translation system for artisans’ everyday business communication. The system is a five-phase cascaded architecture comprising automatic speech recognition (ASR), text normalisation, an intermediate linguistic representation, language-specific translation, and text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis. Its hierarchical staging follows the processing principles of the Hierarchical Efficient Neural Transducer for Speech Recognition and Translation (HENT-SRT), while the neural components of that design are replaced by transparent retrieval mechanisms suited to resource-constrained devices. A domain-specific parallel corpus of 2,000 artisan oriented expressions per target language, built from a needs analysis with artisans in southwestern Nigeria and covering automotive repair, pricing negotiation, service delivery and customer relations, supports translation through exact bilingual lookup, with a fallback to fuzzy retrieval that combines sequence similarity and Jaccard token overlap under a confidence threshold. The system was evaluated on 15 spoken utterances using word error rate (WER) for recognition and BLEU and METEOR for translation, reported at corpus and per-utterance levels with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Yoruba achieved mean BLEU and METEOR of 0.93 and 0.93, and Nigerian Pidgin 0.90 and 0.92. Mean WER was approximately 0.00 on the 14 scorable utterances. Thirteen of 15 utterances (87%) were translated perfectly into both languages; one utterance failed completely and one failed partially in Pidgin. Mean ASR latency was 1.60 s, and translation accounted for less than 1% of end-to-end wall-clock time. The confidence intervals for the two languages overlapped substantially, so no reliable performance difference between them could be established at this sample size. The findings establish the feasibility of a lightweight, transparent speech translation pipeline for in-domain artisan communication and identify numeric expression handling, held out evaluation, and neural extension as the priorities for future work.

papers.title: MedSonor: Learning to Use Clinical Audio in Medical LLMs
papers.abstract: Clinical audio conveys medical information that transcripts may not preserve, but using it in medical responses requires interpreting it alongside clinical requests and dialogue context. Existing medical audio supervision largely targets classification or recognition, while general audio-language models lack specialized medical knowledge and direct feedback for open-ended responses. We present MedSonor, a medical dialogue model integrating medical knowledge, spoken dialogue, and clinical audio understanding. We pair authentic medical audio with clinical requests and combine these audio-integrated dialogues with collected medical audio and synthesized spoken dialogues for supervised fine-tuning, followed by two stages of rubric-guided reinforcement learning. We introduce MedVoice-Dial and MedVoice?AID to evaluate responses within supplied multi-turn medical contexts and to requests involving clinical audio, respectively. Across seven medical benchmarks, MedSonor outperforms the evaluated general-purpose open-weight audio-language baselines and ranks highest in aggregate physician preference evaluation, while broadly retaining general speech capabilities.

papers.title: ConvexLLM: Scaling Convex-Hull Speech Interfaces to General-Purpose Audio Intelligence
papers.abstract: Speech and audio language models connect continuous acoustic representations to decoders pretrained primarily on text data. Most such models use MLP or Q-Former interfaces to map acoustic features into the decoder's input space, requiring the decoder to learn how to interpret the resulting representations. We investigate whether grounding these representations in the decoder's existing text embeddings can help it use acoustic information while better preserving its pretrained text capabilities. We present ConvexLLM, a general-purpose speech and audio language model whose C-Gate interface represents audio as continuous convex combinations of frozen text embeddings. ConvexLLM achieves an eleven-task VoiceBench aggregate of 75.36, the highest among the open-weight models we compare, and an MMAU Test-mini accuracy of 62.50%. Its largest margins over the baselines are on spoken knowledge and reasoning tasks, while the strongest baselines are more accurate on audio understanding and transcription. In a comparison with a 2B-parameter decoder, C-Gate achieves higher aggregate spoken-language performance than MLP and Q-Former interfaces, with text-task performance close to MLP and task-dependent tradeoffs in transcription and audio understanding. These results support convex combinations of text embeddings as a viable interface for general-purpose speech and audio language models.

papers.title: Semantic-Critical Regions for Video-to-Audio Generation
papers.abstract: In real-world videos, sound events are often associated with localized and fine-grained visual cues, such as object motion, object-part dynamics, contact events, and interactions between objects. Existing video-to-audio (V2A) methods employ implicit conditioning based on global visual representations or explicit control derived from temporal and spatial cues. However, subtle sound-producing and sound-indicative interactions remain insufficiently captured, leaving room for more precise visual conditioning of sound-event semantics and temporal dynamics. Motivated by this observation, we refer to regions containing such sound-relevant visual evidence as Semantic-Critical Regions (SCRs) and introduce SCR-V2A, a V2A generation framework that explicitly localizes and encodes SCRs as fine-grained visual guidance for audio generation. Specifically, we first identify SCRs through sound-related visual localization. We then transform the localized regions into a control representation through adapter-based dual visual encoding, which jointly captures global visual context and fine-grained sound-relevant evidence. The representation is used to condition a downstream audio generation model. Experiments on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks demonstrate that SCR-V2A achieves strong performance in distribution matching and audio quality while remaining competitive in cross-modal alignment and requiring few trainable parameters. These results highlight the value of prioritizing fine-grained, sound-relevant visual regions for V2A generation.

papers.title: DriftTTS: One-stage Single Step Text-to-Speech via Generative Drifting
papers.abstract: Text-to-speech models built on score matching and flow matching produce natural speech, but only by calling the decoder many times, which makes synthesis slow. Existing ways to cut the number of calls either distill from a multi-step teacher or add a stage on top of a pretrained model, leaving single-step TTS without a pretrained TTS model unexplored. We question whether pretraining a TTS model is necessary, and propose DriftTTS, which adopts generative drifting, an objective that moves iterative sampling from inference into training. Drifting assumes samples of fixed shape, whereas speech has variable length; we address this issue with segment drifting. On LJSpeech, DriftTTS matches the multi-step quality of Matcha-TTS and RapFlow-TTS in a single decoder call, while being faster. To our knowledge, this is the first application of generative drifting to text-to-speech.
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: text-to-speech

papers.title: MUB: An Identity-Masked Benchmark for Music Understanding in Multimodal Language Models
papers.abstract: Evaluating musical perception in multimodal language models requires separating audio evidence from answers recoverable through metadata or external tools. We present the Music Understanding Benchmark (MUB), a locally assembled collection of 500 identity-masked recordings with existing annotations for tempo, key, time signature, and structural intervals. The collection covers all 24 major/minor key combinations, tempos of 47--180 beats per minute, and 4,676 annotated intervals. Original titles, artists, and platform identifiers are excluded from evaluation inputs. Relative to recent music question-answering and temporal-grounding work, MUB emphasizes scalar tempo prediction and full-recording interval outputs, together with a documented metadata-masking protocol. Saved baseline predictions yield 53.6\% tempo accuracy for a simple DSP estimator and 98.4\% time-signature accuracy for a constant 4/4 predictor. We identify important limitations, including an asymmetric legacy key metric, unverified independent annotation agreement, extreme metre imbalance, and unresolved recording-level rights clearance. No contemporary multimodal language model comparison has yet been completed. MUB is therefore an evaluation resource and protocol under validation, rather than a completed demonstration of model capabilities.
reasons: Music Foundation Models & Representations: music understanding

papers.title: End-to-End VITS Outperforms Two-Stage Tacotron 2 Synthesis for Kazakh: A Comparative Study on a New Multi-Domain Speech Corpus
papers.abstract: Text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis for low-resource languages such as Kazakh is still difficult: the language is agglutinative, uses an extended Cyrillic alphabet and has few annotated speech corpora. We present Kazakh TTS systems trained on a new corpus of about 3000 pages of educational and scientific text from 23 domains, read by two professional speakers. A character-level Tacotron 2 model with guided attention and a Parallel WaveGAN vocoder was trained in ESPnet2 on the female voice, and end-to-end VITS models were trained at 24 kHz for both voices. Guided attention produced a sharp monotonic alignment within 21 epochs. On a new test set of 138 sentences, transcribed with a Kazakh-specific automatic speech recognition (ASR) model, VITS reached a character error rate (CER) of 1.94% (male) and 2.08% (female), against 8.79% for Tacotron 2, whose attention failed on 6.2% of the utterances. On 60 sentences with formulas, numbers and abbreviations, normalised by the system’s text front-end, Tacotron 2 failed on 11.7% of the utterances, while VITS had no failures and lowered the CER from 19.7% to 7.2%. The multilingual Whisper model reported about ten times higher error rates on the same audio, which shows that Whisper is not a reliable intelligibility measure for Kazakh. In a listening test with seven native speakers, Tacotron 2 with Parallel WaveGAN obtained a mean opinion score of 4.5 out of 5 for both naturalness and intelligibility.

papers.title: Beyond the Benchmark: Conditioning, Domains and Failure Modes of Qwen3-TTS
papers.abstract: Qwen3-TTS reports state-of-the-art zero-shot voice cloning, but its technical report leaves open how the model should be conditioned, how it behaves outside read speech, and how it fails. We characterise its two cloning interfaces, in-context learning (ICL) and X-Vector, against Chatterbox, XTTS-v2 and F5-TTS on read, meeting, emotional and air-traffic-control (ATC) speech, using eighteen objective measures, an LLM judge, a spoofing countermeasure and a listening test. Neither interface dominates: ICL clones timbre more closely from correctly transcribed references, X-Vector clones timing, and ICL degrades sharply when a short reference transcript is wrong. Domain explains four times more variance than system choice. Qwen3-TTS leads on intelligibility and pitch register but trails on prosody, and the objective measures rank systems differently from listeners. An off-the-shelf countermeasure flags its clones no more often than genuine recordings, and on ATC radio it fails for every system. Code and audio are released.
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: voice cloning

papers.title: Audio System One Model: Typed Probabilistic Perception of Emotion in Speech
papers.abstract: Speech applications ask many questions about the same voice: which emotion a listener perceives, how aroused the speaker sounds, whether they sound frustrated. Classifiers answer fast, over one fixed label set; audio language models (ALMs) take any question in text, but answer by generation, one pass per question, with poorly calibrated probabilities. We present ASOM (Audio System One Model), a System One model for speech: choice, score and yes/no questions written at request time are answered in one pass, without generation, each with a probability distribution. Frozen speech and text encoders feed a 6.2M-parameter reader with no per-class parameters, trained on listener vote distributions. On MSP-Podcast, ASOM matches a classifier on the same features and data, leads the best of 6 zero-shot ALMs by 0.072 and an ALM fine-tuned on the same data by 0.026, and answers 20 questions in 13.1 ms, 17-41 times faster than the ALMs. It also answers reworded, reduced and new label sets, scales and gender, and on 21 unseen corpora in 13 languages it leads the best zero-shot ALM by 0.138 where the words carry no emotion; where they do, the ALMs mostly read.
reasons: Audio & Speech Language Models: audio language model

# ACE-Step 1.5, MLX 8-bit (language model and DiT)

8-bit MLX versions of the three large parts of [ACE-Step 1.5](https://github.com/ace-step/ACE-Step-1.5) by ACE Studio
and StepFun, for Apple Silicon: the 5 Hz language model (1.7B) and the DiT decoders of `acestep-v15-turbo` and
`acestep-v15-base`. They are used by Audante Link, the desktop helper of the music app Audante, so that ACE-Step 1.5
runs on Macs with 24 to 32 GB of memory. **This is not an official ACE-Step release.**

The files need ACE-Step 1.5's own code (commit `ca1e85fe9430179831e6bc6be790c332190a3866`) with Audante's patch
[`ace-step-mlx-quant.patch`](ace-step-mlx-quant.patch): upstream converts the DiT from PyTorch at start-up and has no
way to load a pre-quantized one.

## Contents

| Folder | File | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `acestep-5Hz-lm-1.7B/` | `model.safetensors` (1.97 GB) | the language model, 8-bit |
| | `config.json` | the original plus a `quantization` entry |
| | tokenizer files, `chat_template.jinja` | unchanged |
| `acestep-v15-turbo/` | `mlx_dit.safetensors` (1.78 GB), `mlx_dit.json` | the DiT decoder in MLX, 8-bit |
| | `model.safetensors` (1.64 GB) | the original without the decoder: lyric and timbre encoders, audio tokenizer and detokenizer, bf16 |
| | `config.json`, `silence_latent.pt`, model code | unchanged |
| `acestep-v15-base/` | the same files for the base DiT (add a track, accompaniment) | |

Not included, unchanged in [ACE-Step/Ace-Step1.5](https://huggingface.co/ACE-Step/Ace-Step1.5): the VAE (`vae/`), the
text encoder (`Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B/`) and the top-level `config.json`. To use the files, put these three folders
over a download of the original (base goes into `acestep-v15-base/`) and apply the patch to ACE-Step 1.5.

## Changes made by Audante (19.10.2026)

Source: [ACE-Step/Ace-Step1.5](https://huggingface.co/ACE-Step/Ace-Step1.5) at revision
`19671f406d603126926c1b7e2adc169acbcade22` and [ACE-Step/acestep-v15-base](https://huggingface.co/ACE-Step/acestep-v15-base)
at revision `e432212fec32b8965a14ffa57ae653438d6abd14`. No retraining, no fine-tuning.

- **Language model:** loaded with mlx-lm 0.29.1 (`model.` prefix added to the key names, as ACE-Step does when it
  loads the original) and quantized with mlx-lm's `quantize_model`: every linear layer and the tied embedding (which
  is also the output layer) at 8 bits, affine, group size 64 (8.5 bits per weight on average). `config.json` gets
  `"quantization": {"group_size": 64, "bits": 8, "mode": "affine"}`.
- **DiT decoders (turbo and base):** the `decoder.*` tensors of `model.safetensors` (bf16) are rearranged the way
  ACE-Step's own `acestep/models/mlx/dit_convert.py` does it at start-up, cast to float32 and loaded into ACE-Step's
  `MLXDiTDecoder`. Every linear layer is quantized to 8 bits, affine, group size 64 (the timestep embeddings as
  well); convolutions, norms and the AdaLN tables stay float32, as ACE-Step runs them. The result is
  `mlx_dit.safetensors`; `mlx_dit.json` records bits, group size and the 8-bit layers. `model.safetensors` keeps
  all other tensors unchanged.
- The model code (`*.py`), `config.json` of the DiTs, `silence_latent.pt` and the tokenizer files are byte-identical
  to the originals. `SHA256SUMS` lists every file.

The patch makes ACE-Step load `mlx_dit.safetensors` when it is there and leave its PyTorch copy of the decoder
empty, and it loads the 8-bit language model with mlx-lm's `load_model`. It also adds settings Audante uses with the
original files: a cap on MLX's buffer cache (`ACESTEP_MLX_CACHE_GB`), freeing the unused PyTorch decoder
(`ACESTEP_FREE_TORCH_DIT=1`, the audio stays byte-identical), a seed for the language model of a single song
(`ACESTEP_MLX_LM_SEED=1`; upstream seeds it only in batches) and no model downloads at run time
(`ACESTEP_NO_DOWNLOAD=1`).

## Measured

On a Mac Studio (M3 Ultra) with ACE-Step's API server at commit `ca1e85f` and the patch, ACE-Step set up as on a
32-GB Mac (`MAX_MPS_VRAM=21.3`), MLX cache 0.5 GB, a fixed seed, one song at 30 and 180 seconds. Peak = lifetime
maximum of the server's physical footprint, GPU memory included.

| | Disk (without base) | Peak 30 s · 180 s |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Original files, as upstream loads them | 10.1 GB | 55.8 · 60.7 GB |
| Original files, MLX cache capped | 10.1 GB | 31.7 · 32.8 GB |
| Original files, unused PyTorch decoder freed | 10.1 GB | 26.3 · 26.6 GB |
| **These files** | **7.0 GB** | **20.2 · 20.3 GB** |

As on a 24-GB Mac (`MAX_MPS_VRAM=16`, CPU offload off), these files peak at 17.3 GB (30 s) and 17.5 GB (180 s).
With the base DiT loaded as a second model for add-track, the server peaked at 29.7 GB instead of 42.8 GB with the
original files (decoder freed).

Sound and fidelity, against the original files with the same seed:

- **DiT (turbo), 8-bit:** with identical language-model codes, mean log-mel distance 0.31 dB (30 s) and 0.46 dB
  (180 s), waveform SNR 17 and 21 dB.
- **Language model, 8-bit:** against bf16 on the same 901 audio codes and 166 metadata tokens (teacher forcing): mean
  KL divergence 0.052 on the codes (0.18 with classifier-free guidance), 0.012 on the metadata; negative log
  likelihood 6.57 instead of 6.52. Because ACE-Step samples the codes at temperature 0.85, any change of the
  language model makes a different song from the same seed.
- **DiT (base), 8-bit:** adding a drum track to the same 30-s song with the same seed: 1.03 dB log-mel distance and
  17.5 dB SNR for the new track alone, 0.47 dB for the mix (two runs of the original differ by 0.05 dB). This is
  more than the turbo DiT; the base DiT runs 32 steps with guidance.
- Speed: the 8-bit language model writes the codes of a 3-minute song in 9.1 instead of 13.0 seconds; the DiT is as
  fast as before.

English | 简体中文

**MOSS-Music** is an open-source **music understanding model** from [MOSI.AI](https://mosi.cn/#hero), the [OpenMOSS team](https://www.open-moss.com/), and [Shanghai Innovation Institute](https://www.sii.edu.cn/). Built on the same audio backbone as [MOSS-Audio](https://github.com/OpenMOSS/MOSS-Audio), MOSS-Music is further specialised on music via dedicated continual pre-training and supervised fine-tuning — targeting **musical captioning, lyrics ASR, structural analysis, chord / key / tempo reasoning, and long-form musical question answering**. In this release, we provide **two 8B models**: **MOSS-Music-8B-Instruct** and **MOSS-Music-8B-Thinking**. The Instruct variant is optimised for direct instruction following on musical prompts, while the Thinking variant provides stronger chain-of-thought reasoning for musical analysis. ## News * 2026.05.01: 🎉🎉🎉 We have released [MOSS-Music](https://github.com/OpenMOSS/MOSS-Music). * 2026.05.01: 🎉🎉🎉 We have released [MOSS-Music-Data-Pipeline](https://github.com/wx9songs/MOSS-Music-Data-Pipeline) for large-scale music data annotation and processing. ## Contents - [Introduction](#introduction) - [Model Architecture](#model-architecture) - [DeepStack Cross-Layer Feature Injection](#deepstack-cross-layer-feature-injection) - [Time-Aware Representation](#time-aware-representation) - [Released Models](#released-models) - [Music Data Pipeline](#music-data-pipeline) - [Evaluation](#evaluation) - [Quickstart](#quickstart) - [Environment Setup](#environment-setup) - [SGLang Serving](#sglang-serving) - [Gradio App](#gradio-app) - [More Information](#more-information) - [LICENSE](#license) - [Citation](#citation) ## Introduction Music is not just audio plus lyrics — understanding it requires perceiving harmonic structure, rhythm, timbre, instrumentation, performance nuance, and the textual content of the lyrics, and reasoning about them jointly across time. **MOSS-Music** is built to unify these capabilities within a single model. - **Lyrics ASR & time-aligned transcription**: Accurate singing ASR with sentence- and word-level timestamps, robust to backing tracks. - **Musical captioning & tagging**: Natural-language descriptions of mood, genre, instrumentation, production style, and emotional trajectory. - **Key / tempo / chord reasoning**: Identifies musical key, beats, downbeats, and chord progressions, including timestamped chord transcription. - **Structural analysis**: Segments a song into intro / verse / chorus / bridge / outro and reasons about repetition and contrast. - **Instrument & voice recognition**: Identifies prominent instruments and singing voices (solo / chorus, gender, register). - **Musical QA and long-form analysis**: Open-ended question answering grounded in a full track, including chain-of-thought reasoning in the *Thinking* variant.

## Model Architecture MOSS-Music inherits the MOSS-Audio modular design, comprising three components: an audio encoder, a modality adapter, and a large language model. Raw audio is first encoded by **MOSS-Audio-Encoder** into continuous temporal representations at **12.5 Hz**, which are then projected into the language model's embedding space through the adapter and finally consumed by the LLM for auto-regressive text generation. Rather than relying on off-the-shelf audio frontends, we train a dedicated encoder from scratch to obtain more robust acoustic representations, tighter temporal alignment, and better extensibility across musical styles, singing, and non-speech acoustic content. ### DeepStack Cross-Layer Feature Injection Using only the encoder's top-layer features tends to lose low-level prosody, transient events, and local time-frequency structure. To address this, we adopt a **DeepStack**-inspired cross-layer injection module between the encoder and the language model: in addition to the encoder's final-layer output, features from earlier and intermediate layers are selected, independently projected, and injected into the language model's early layers, preserving multi-granularity information from low-level acoustic details to high-level semantic abstractions. This design is especially well-suited for music understanding, as it helps retain rhythm, timbre, transients, and instrumental texture — information that a single high-level representation cannot fully capture, yet is critical for chord recognition, structural analysis, and nuanced musical description. ### Time-Aware Representation Time is a critical dimension in music understanding. To enhance explicit temporal awareness, we adopt a **time-marker insertion** strategy during pre-training: explicit time tokens are inserted between audio frame representations at fixed time intervals to indicate temporal positions. This design enables the model to learn "what happened when" within a unified text generation framework, naturally supporting timestamped lyrics ASR, beat / downbeat localisation, section boundary detection, and long-song retrospective QA. Ming-3.0-audio-flash

Hear clearly. Understand deeply. Act intelligently.

Ming-3.0-audio-flash is a native audio-language model from inclusionAI. It accepts audio together with text instructions and supports speech recognition, spoken question answering, audio understanding, audio reasoning, and optional synthesized-speech responses.
GitHub · 🤖 ModelScope · 🤗 Flash · 🤗 Tiny · 💻 Examples
## Model Summary | Property | Description | | --- | --- | | Developer | inclusionAI | | Model type | Native audio-language Mixture-of-Experts model | | Parameters | 126B total parameters, 6.5B activated per inference step | | Inputs | Audio and text instructions | | Outputs | Text, or text with optional synthesized speech | | Primary languages | Chinese and English, including varied accents and dialects | | License | MIT | ## Highlights - **Complex speech recognition:** Handles Chinese and English speech, dialects, accents, noisy environments, and multi-speaker recordings. - **Long-audio understanding:** Comprehends and analyzes long-form recordings. - **Multidimensional perception:** Understands speech, non-speech sounds, acoustic scenes, and music. - **Audio reasoning:** Answers questions and performs reasoning over audio content. - **Audio interaction:** Produces text responses and can optionally synthesize speech with built-in voices or a reference voice. ## Architecture Ming-3.0-audio-flash combines an audio encoder and projector with a Mixture-of-Experts language backbone. An optional Talker generates speech responses from the model's output.

## Quick Start with Transformers The model uses custom Transformers code. Review the repository code before enabling `trust_remote_code=True`. ```bash git clone https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash.git cd Ming-3.0-audio-flash python -m venv .venv-transformers source .venv-transformers/bin/activate pip install -r requirements-transformers.txt ``` ### Audio Understanding ```bash python examples/transformers_audio.py examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav \ --model inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash \ --prompt "Please answer the question in the audio." ``` ### Speech Recognition ```bash python examples/transformers_audio.py examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav \ --model inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash \ --task asr \ --max-new-tokens 256 \ --no-repeat-ngram-size 10 ``` The validated ASR prompt asks the model to identify the spoken language and place a tab between the language label and transcription. ### Direct Python Usage ```python import torch from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash" audio_path = "examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained( model_id, trust_remote_code=True, use_fast=False, ) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto", trust_remote_code=True, ).eval() messages = [ { "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "audio", "audio": audio_path}, {"type": "text", "text": "Please answer the question in the audio."}, ], } ] inputs = processor(messages).to(model.device) inputs["audio_feats"] = inputs["audio_feats"].to(model.dtype) with torch.inference_mode(): output_ids = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens=512, do_sample=False, ) generated_ids = output_ids[0, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1] :] response = processor.decode(generated_ids, skip_special_tokens=True).strip() print(response) ``` ## Speech Output The Talker example supports built-in voices and reference-audio voice prompting: ```bash python examples/transformers_thinker_talker.py \ --model inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash \ --audio examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav \ --voice US_Stella \ --output output.wav ``` See the [voice guide](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash/blob/main/docs/voices.md) for available voice names and reference-audio usage. ## Serving ### vLLM-Omni ```bash export MODEL_PATH=inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash MING_OUTPUT_MODE=text ./scripts/serve_vllm_omni.sh "$MODEL_PATH" ``` The reference 128K serving profile uses tensor parallelism across eight 80 GB H800 GPUs. Select the deployment YAML that matches text-only or Talker output. See the [deployment guide](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash/blob/main/README.md#vllm-omni) for details. For speech output, start the audio profile and select an IP or registered voice with the vLLM-Omni client's `--voice` option: ```bash MING_OUTPUT_MODE=audio ./scripts/serve_vllm_omni.sh "$MODEL_PATH" python examples/vllm_omni_audio_chat.py examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav \ --audio-response \ --voice US_Stella \ --output-audio outputs/answer.wav ``` The client sends this selection as Chat Completions `audio.voice: {"id": "..."}`. vLLM-Omni uses the built-in IP voice `灵小柔` when no voice is specified. The model directory also provides `灵楷` and `US_James` as preset reference voices under `voice_presets/voice_audio/`, with their matching transcripts in `voice_presets/voice_prompts.json`. Both names are also available as built-in IP voices. ### SGLang ```bash export MODEL_PATH=inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash ./scripts/serve_sglang.sh "$MODEL_PATH" ``` The validated SGLang profile uses four GPUs and provides text output. See the [SGLang example](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash/blob/main/examples/sglang_audio_chat.py) for client usage. ## Evaluation ### Speech Recognition

Ming-3.0-audio-tiny

Hear clearly. Understand deeply. Act intelligently.

Ming-3.0-audio-tiny is a compact native audio-language model from inclusionAI. It accepts audio together with text instructions and supports speech recognition, spoken question answering, audio understanding, audio reasoning, and optional synthesized-speech responses.
GitHub · 🤗 Flash · 🤗 Tiny · 💻 Examples
## Model Summary | Property | Description | | --- | --- | | Developer | inclusionAI | | Model type | Compact native audio-language Mixture-of-Experts model | | Parameters | 9.3B total parameters, 2.7B activated per inference step | | Inputs | Audio and text instructions | | Outputs | Text, or text with optional synthesized speech | | Primary languages | Chinese and English, including varied accents and dialects | | License | MIT | ## Highlights - **Efficient audio intelligence:** Provides speech and audio understanding in a compact Mixture-of-Experts model. - **Complex speech recognition:** Handles Chinese and English speech, dialects, accents, noisy environments, and multi-speaker recordings. - **Long-audio understanding:** Comprehends and analyzes long-form recordings. - **Multidimensional perception:** Understands speech, non-speech sounds, acoustic scenes, and music. - **Audio reasoning:** Answers questions and performs reasoning over audio content. - **Audio interaction:** Produces text responses and can optionally synthesize speech with built-in voices or a reference voice. ## Architecture Ming-3.0-audio-tiny combines an audio encoder and projector with a compact Mixture-of-Experts language backbone. An optional Talker generates speech responses from the model's output. ## Quick Start with Transformers The model uses custom Transformers code. Review the repository code before enabling `trust_remote_code=True`. ```bash git clone https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash.git cd Ming-3.0-audio-flash python -m venv .venv-transformers source .venv-transformers/bin/activate pip install -r requirements-transformers.txt ``` ### Audio Understanding ```bash python examples/transformers_audio.py examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav \ --model inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-tiny \ --prompt "Please answer the question in the audio." ``` ### Speech Recognition ```bash python examples/transformers_audio.py examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav \ --model inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-tiny \ --task asr \ --max-new-tokens 256 \ --no-repeat-ngram-size 10 ``` The validated ASR prompt asks the model to identify the spoken language and place a tab between the language label and transcription. ### Direct Python Usage ```python import torch from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-tiny" audio_path = "examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained( model_id, trust_remote_code=True, use_fast=False, ) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto", trust_remote_code=True, ).eval() messages = [ { "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "audio", "audio": audio_path}, {"type": "text", "text": "Please answer the question in the audio."}, ], } ] inputs = processor(messages).to(model.device) inputs["audio_feats"] = inputs["audio_feats"].to(model.dtype) with torch.inference_mode(): output_ids = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens=512, do_sample=False, ) generated_ids = output_ids[0, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1] :] response = processor.decode(generated_ids, skip_special_tokens=True).strip() print(response) ``` ## Speech Output The Talker example supports built-in voices and reference-audio voice prompting: ```bash python examples/transformers_thinker_talker.py \ --model inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-tiny \ --audio examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav \ --ip-name US_Stella \ --output output.wav ``` See the [voice guide](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash/blob/main/docs/voices.md) for available voice names, invocation rules, and reference-audio usage. ## Serving ### vLLM-Omni Text output or ASR uses the Tiny Thinker on one GPU: ```bash export MODEL_PATH=inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-tiny MING_MODEL_VARIANT=tiny MING_OUTPUT_MODE=text \ ./scripts/serve_vllm_omni.sh "$MODEL_PATH" ``` For synthesized-speech output, select the full-audio profile: ```bash export MODEL_PATH=inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-tiny MING_MODEL_VARIANT=tiny MING_OUTPUT_MODE=audio \ ./scripts/serve_vllm_omni.sh "$MODEL_PATH" ``` The reference full-audio profile places the Thinker on GPU 0 and the Talker on GPU 1. Select the deployment YAML that matches text-only, ASR, or Talker output. See the [deployment guide](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash/blob/main/README.md#vllm-omni) for details. Both names are also available as built-in IP voices. ### SGLang ```bash export MODEL_PATH=inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-tiny MING_MODEL_VARIANT=tiny CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 \ ./scripts/serve_sglang.sh "$MODEL_PATH" ``` The validated Tiny SGLang profile uses one GPU and provides text output. Ming-3.0-tts-tiny

7.9B-A1.3B multilingual MoE speech synthesis with paralinguistic and free-form control.

GitHub | Blog & Demos | ModelScope

This repository contains **Ming-3.0-tts-tiny**, the Ming-3.0-tts mixture-of-experts checkpoint built on Ling V3. Its Ling V3 backbone has 7.9B total parameters and activates about 1.3B parameters per token. The repository includes sharded weights, supporting model code, audio tokenizer, speaker encoder and text tokenizer. > **Inference requires the [Ming-3.0-tts GitHub repository](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts).** This Hugging Face repository is for checkpoint distribution and does not provide a standalone inference setup. Clone the GitHub repository and follow its README for the current dependencies, inference code and usage instructions. The CLI scripts and Python APIs referenced below are provided by the GitHub repository. ## Model Details | Item | Value | | --- | --- | | Architecture | Mixture of Experts, Ling V3 backbone | | Backbone parameters | 7.9B total, about 1.3B active per token | | Languages | Chinese, English, German, Spanish, French, Korean, Japanese | | Dialects | Sichuanese, Cantonese | | Python API | `ming_tiny.MingTinyTTS` | | CLI | `infer_tiny.py` | | Prompt protocol | `thinking_v1` | ## Capabilities - Zero-shot voice cloning from a short reference clip - Voice Design from a natural-language speaker description - Free-form control of delivery and speaking style - 100+ built-in Chinese voices and five built-in English voices - Multilingual synthesis and Sichuanese/Cantonese dialect control - 14 inline tags for breath, cough, sigh, laughter, hesitation, surprise and question/confirmation sounds in Chinese or English - Explicit emotion, speed, pitch and volume control - Multi-speaker dialogue from a script and speaker references (`podcast`)

## Quick Start ### Installation ```bash git clone https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts.git cd Ming-3.0-tts conda create -n ming-tiny python=3.10.15 -y conda activate ming-tiny pip install -r requirements-tiny.txt ``` Tiny uses a separate reference inference environment: Python **3.10.15**, PyTorch and torchaudio **2.7.1+cu118** (CUDA 11.8 wheels), and `transformers==4.46.3`. Install the pinned dependencies from [requirements-tiny.txt](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts/blob/main/requirements-tiny.txt) in a dedicated environment, as other dependency versions differ from 0.5B. We recommend using NVIDIA H800 for inference. ### Download ```bash pip install "huggingface_hub[cli]" hf download inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts-tiny --local-dir Ming-3.0-tts-tiny ``` ### CLI Inference ```bash python infer_tiny.py \ --model_path inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts-tiny \ --task dialect \ --text "今日天气几好，我哋食完饭一齐去海边行下啦。" \ --dialect 广粤话 \ --prompt_wav data/wavs/10002287-00000094.wav \ --output_path output/tiny.wav ``` ### Python API Loading configures the release runtime (bf16, portable MoE loop, fp32 recurrent state) and checks the checkpoint against it; `generate()` defaults to `cfg_scale=2.0`, `temperature=0`, `flow_steps=10`, and `sigma=0.25`. ```python from ming_tiny import MingTinyTTS tts = MingTinyTTS.from_pretrained("inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts-tiny", device="cuda:0") tts.generate( task="seed", text="傍晚的风从山口吹过来，远处的云慢慢染成了金色。", prompt_wav="data/wavs/10002287-00000094.wav", prompt_text="在此奉劝大家别乱打美白针。", target_language="Chinese", # English for English text output_path="outputs/seed.wav", ) ``` ### Supported Tasks Each call selects one task and accepts the inputs listed below: | Task | Reference audio | Reference text | `target_language` | Controls | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `seed` | one | required | `Chinese` / `English`, required | — | | `multilingual` | one | required | `German` / `Spanish` / `French` / `Korean` / `Japanese` | — | | `paralinguistic` | one | required | `Chinese` / `English` | inline tags in `text` | | `podcast` | one per speaker | one per speaker, same order | inferred from the text | `speaker_N:` at the start of every line | | `basic` | one | not accepted | — | `speed`, `pitch`, `volume`, all three | | `emotion` | one | not accepted | — | `emotion` | | `dialect` | one | not accepted | — | `dialect`: `川渝话` / `广粤话` | | `freeform` | one | not accepted | — | `instruction` | | `voice_design` | none | — | — | `style` | | `ip` | none | — | — | `ip` | Freeform always requires a reference clip and cannot be combined with voice design, a built-in voice, emotion, dialect or attribute controls. For `podcast`, start every dialogue line with `speaker_N:` and provide one reference audio clip and transcript per speaker, in speaker order. Repeat `--prompt_wav` and `--prompt_text` on the command line. See the [Tiny examples](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts#ming-30-tts-tiny) for a Podcast Python example and [examples/one_click/](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts/tree/main/examples/one_click) for scripts for every task. `python infer_tiny.py --help` lists the CLI arguments. ### Verify the Checkpoint ```bash python tools/preflight_tiny.py --model_path /path/to/Ming-3.0-tts-tiny ``` ## Performance Benchmark comparisons from the [project README](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts#performance). **Bold** and underline mark the best and second-best values among the listed open-source models; ties share a mark. Confucius4-TTS: a Multilingual and Cross-Lingual Zero-Shot TTS Engine

One voice. Any language.

                                       

Confucius4-TTS is an advanced LLM-based text-to-speech (TTS) system designed for multilingual and cross-lingual speech synthesis. Built on a speech encoder + large language model (LLM) architecture, Confucius4-TTS enables high-quality speech generation while preserving speaker identity across languages. You can try our online demo at **[https://confucius4-tts.youdao.com/gradio](https://confucius4-tts.youdao.com/gradio)**. **✨ Key Features** - **14 Languages Supported**: Chinese, English, Japanese, Korean, German, French, Spanish, Indonesian, Italian, Thai, Portuguese, Russian, Malay and Vietnamese *(more coming soon)* - **Unconstrained Voice Cloning**: No reference transcript required - **Cross-Lingual Voice Transfer**: Unaccented speech synthesis across 14 languages - **Zero-Shot Voice Transfer**: Clone voices without additional training - **Seamless Emotion Transfer**: Clone the feeling, not just the voice - **Robust Generalization**: Stable performance in real-world multilingual scenarios With strong cross-lingual generalization, Confucius4-TTS allows users to seamlessly switch languages while keeping the same voice, delivering fluent, natural, and expressive speech. ## Contents - [Installation](#-installation) - [Inference](#-inference) - [Training](#-training) - [Performance](#-performance) - [Citation](#citation) ## 🛠 Installation ### Requirements - Python 3.10 - CUDA 12.6 ### Setup 1. Clone the repository: ```bash git clone https://github.com/netease-youdao/Confucius4-TTS.git cd Confucius4-TTS ``` 2. Create and activate a conda environment: ```bash conda create -n confuciustts python=3.10 -y conda activate confuciustts ``` 3. Install dependencies: ```bash pip install -r requirements.txt ``` ## 🚀 Inference Use the provided `example.py` script for zero-shot TTS synthesis: ```bash python example.py \ --prompt_wav path/to/reference.wav \ --text "Your text to synthesize" \ --lang en \ --out output.wav \ --config config/inference_config.yaml ``` You can also use the Python API directly: ```python import torch import torchaudio from confuciustts.cli.inference import ConfuciusTTS model = ConfuciusTTS( config_path="config/inference_config.yaml", device="cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu", ) audio = model.generate( text="Hello, welcome to Confucius4-TTS.", lang="en", prompt_wav="path/to/reference.wav", verbose=True, ) torchaudio.save("output.wav", audio.cpu(), model.sample_rate) ``` ## 🚀 Fine-Tuning Confucius4-TTS follows a "speech encoder + LLM" architecture. The training pipeline covers two modules: - **Text2Semantic (T2S)**: generates semantic token sequences from text and speaker conditioning. - **Semantic2Acoustic (S2A)**: a flow-matching model that converts semantic tokens into mel spectrograms. ### 1. Prepare Pretrained Models Download the two external models: ```bash # Wav2Vec2-BERT (speaker conditioning & semantic feature extraction) huggingface-cli download facebook/w2v-bert-2.0 \ --local-dir pretrained/w2v-bert-2.0 # Amphion MaskGCT (semantic codec implementation) git clone https://github.com/open-mmlab/Amphion.git external/Amphion ``` After downloading, your directory should look like: ``` checkpoints/ ├── t2s_model.safetensors # pretrained T2S weights ├── s2a_model.pt # pretrained S2A weights ├── wav2vec2bert_stats.pt # semantic feature normalization statistics ├── special_tokens_map.json # tokenizer files ├── tokenizer.json ├── tokenizer.model └── tokenizer_config.json pretrained/ ├── w2v-bert-2.0/ # Wav2Vec2-BERT model └── campplus/ └── campplus_cn_common.bin # CAMPPlus speaker encoder checkpoint external/ └── Amphion/ # MaskGCT semantic codec implementation ``` ### 2. Prepare Training Data Training data is provided as **TSV files** (tab-separated, no header) with the following 5 columns: | Column | Description | |---|---| | `lang` | Language code (e.g. `zh`, `en`, `ja`) | | `wav_path` | Path to the target audio | | `norm_text` | Normalized text | | `semantic_ids_path` | Pre-extracted semantic tokens (`.npy` file path) | | `ref_audio_paths` | Reference audio path(s), comma-separated for multiple | Configure the train/validation paths in `config/train_t2s.yaml`: ```yaml data: train_data_path: - data/train.tsv val_data_path: - data/val.tsv ``` ### 3. Launch T2S Training Set the pretrained T2S checkpoint path in `config/train_t2s.yaml`: ```yaml paths: t2s_checkpoint: checkpoints/t2s_model.safetensors ``` **Single-node training:** ```bash python -m confuciustts.cli.train_t2s -c config/train_t2s.yaml ``` ### 4. Launch S2A Training Set the checkpoint paths in `config/train_s2a.yaml`. `t2s_checkpoint` points to the frozen T2S backbone; `s2a_checkpoint` is optional and can be used to resume from a pretrained S2A model: ```yaml paths: t2s_checkpoint: checkpoints/t2s_model.safetensors s2a_checkpoint: checkpoints/s2a_model.pt # optional: resume from pretrained S2A ``` **Single-node training:** ```bash python -m confuciustts.cli.train_s2a -c config/train_s2a.yaml ``` During S2A training, the T2S model, speaker encoder (Wav2Vec2-BERT), and style encoder (CAMPPlus) are all frozen. Only the flow-matching S2A model is trained. ## 📊 Performance Confucius4-TTS achieves competitive results on multilingual and cross-lingual zero-shot TTS benchmarks, with strong intelligibility and speaker similarity across multiple languages. > Lower is better for WER/CER (↓), and higher is better for SIM (↑). ### CV3-eval Cross-lingual

Ming-3.0-tts-0.5B

Dense 0.5B multilingual speech synthesis with paralinguistic and free-form control.

GitHub | Blog & Demos | ModelScope

This repository contains **Ming-3.0-tts-0.5B**, the dense Ming-3.0-tts checkpoint built on Qwen2.5-0.5B. The checkpoint includes the backbone, DiT head, audio tokenizer, speaker encoder and text tokenizer. > **Inference requires the [Ming-3.0-tts GitHub repository](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts).** This Hugging Face repository is for checkpoint distribution and does not provide a standalone inference setup. Clone the GitHub repository and follow its README for the current dependencies, inference code and usage instructions. The CLI scripts and Python APIs referenced below are provided by the GitHub repository. ## Model Details | Item | Value | | --- | --- | | Architecture | Dense, Qwen2.5-0.5B backbone | | Parameters | 0.5B | | Languages | Chinese, English, German, Spanish, French, Korean, Japanese | | Dialects | Sichuanese, Cantonese | | Python API | `ming_tts.MingTTS` | | CLI | `infer.py` | | Sample rate | 44.1 kHz | ## Capabilities - Zero-shot voice cloning from a short reference clip - Voice Design from a natural-language speaker description - Free-form control of delivery and speaking style - 100+ built-in Chinese voices and five built-in English voices - 14 inline tags for breath, cough, sigh, laughter, hesitation, surprise and question/confirmation sounds in Chinese or English - Explicit emotion, speed, pitch and volume control - Multilingual synthesis and Sichuanese/Cantonese dialect control

## Quick Start ### Installation ```bash git clone https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts.git cd Ming-3.0-tts pip install -r requirements.txt ``` Tested on NVIDIA H800-80GB and H20-96G with CUDA 12.4. `flash-attn` is optional; inference falls back to PyTorch SDPA. Numbers, dates, units and symbols are normalized with FST grammars. Install `pynini`, or pass `--no_text_normalization` to skip text normalization: ```bash conda install -c conda-forge pynini==2.1.6 ``` ### Download ```bash pip install "huggingface_hub[cli]" hf download inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts-0.5B --local-dir Ming-3.0-tts-0.5b ``` ### CLI Inference ```bash python infer.py \ --model_path inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts-0.5B \ --task TTS \ --language_id Chinese \ --text "傍晚的风从山口吹过来，远处的云慢慢染成了金色。" \ --prompt_wav_path data/wavs/10002287-00000094.wav \ --prompt_text "在此奉劝大家别乱打美白针。" \ --use_spk_emb \ --output output/tts.wav ``` ### Python API ```python from ming_tts import MingTTS model = MingTTS("inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts-0.5B") model.synthesize( task="TTS", language_id="Chinese", # English for English text text="傍晚的风从山口吹过来，远处的云慢慢染成了金色。", prompt_wav_path="data/wavs/10002287-00000094.wav", prompt_text="在此奉劝大家别乱打美白针。", use_spk_emb=True, output_path="output/tts.wav", ) ``` Supported tasks are `TTS`, `FREEFORM`, `VOICE_DESIGN`, `MULTILINGUAL`, `BASIC`, `EMOTION`, `DIALECT` and `IP`. See the [task cookbook](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts/blob/main/cookbooks/instructions.md) for controls and examples. `MULTILINGUAL` requires `language_id` for German, Spanish, French, Korean or Japanese; `DIALECT` takes no language ID. Freeform uses its own task and cannot be combined with voice design, a built-in voice, emotion, dialect or attribute controls. With a reference clip it follows that voice; without a reference, the instruction can choose the voice. ### Verify the Checkpoint ```bash python tools/preflight.py --model_path /path/to/Ming-3.0-tts-0.5b ``` ## Performance Benchmark comparisons from the [project README](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts#performance). **Bold** and underline mark the best and second-best values among the listed open-source models; ties share a mark. Ming-3.0-tts-tiny

GitHub | Blog & Demos | ModelScope

This repository contains **Ming-3.0-tts-tiny**, the Ming-3.0-tts mixture-of-experts checkpoint built on Ling V3. Its Ling V3 backbone has 7.9B total parameters and activates about 1.3B parameters per token. The repository includes sharded weights, supporting model code, audio tokenizer, speaker encoder and text tokenizer. > **Inference requires the [Ming-3.0-tts GitHub repository](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts).** This Hugging Face repository is for checkpoint distribution and does not provide a standalone inference setup. Clone the GitHub repository and follow its README for the current dependencies, inference code and usage instructions. The CLI scripts and Python APIs referenced below are provided by the GitHub repository. ## Model Details | Item | Value | | --- | --- | | Architecture | Mixture of Experts, Ling V3 backbone | | Backbone parameters | 7.9B total, about 1.3B active per token | | Languages | Chinese, English, German, Spanish, French, Korean, Japanese | | Dialects | Sichuanese, Cantonese | | Python API | `ming_tiny.MingTinyTTS` | | CLI | `infer_tiny.py` | | Prompt protocol | `thinking_v1` | ## Capabilities - Zero-shot voice cloning from a short reference clip - Voice Design from a natural-language speaker description - Free-form control of delivery and speaking style - 100+ built-in Chinese voices and five built-in English voices - Multilingual synthesis and Sichuanese/Cantonese dialect control - 14 inline tags for breath, cough, sigh, laughter, hesitation, surprise and question/confirmation sounds in Chinese or English - Explicit emotion, speed, pitch and volume control - Multi-speaker dialogue from a script and speaker references (`podcast`)

## Quick Start ### Installation ```bash git clone https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts.git cd Ming-3.0-tts conda create -n ming-tiny python=3.10.15 -y conda activate ming-tiny pip install -r requirements-tiny.txt ``` Tiny uses a separate reference inference environment: Python **3.10.15**, PyTorch and torchaudio **2.7.1+cu118** (CUDA 11.8 wheels), and `transformers==4.46.3`. Install the pinned dependencies from [requirements-tiny.txt](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts/blob/main/requirements-tiny.txt) in a dedicated environment, as other dependency versions differ from 0.5B. We recommend using NVIDIA H800 for inference. ### Download ```bash pip install "huggingface_hub[cli]" hf download inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts-tiny --local-dir Ming-3.0-tts-tiny ``` ### CLI Inference ```bash python infer_tiny.py \ --model_path inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts-tiny \ --task dialect \ --text "今日天气几好，我哋食完饭一齐去海边行下啦。" \ --dialect 广粤话 \ --prompt_wav data/wavs/10002287-00000094.wav \ --output_path output/tiny.wav ``` ### Python API Loading configures the release runtime (bf16, portable MoE loop, fp32 recurrent state) and checks the checkpoint against it; `generate()` defaults to `cfg_scale=2.0`, `temperature=0`, `flow_steps=10`, and `sigma=0.25`. ```python from ming_tiny import MingTinyTTS tts = MingTinyTTS.from_pretrained("inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts-tiny", device="cuda:0") tts.generate( task="seed", text="傍晚的风从山口吹过来，远处的云慢慢染成了金色。", prompt_wav="data/wavs/10002287-00000094.wav", prompt_text="在此奉劝大家别乱打美白针。", target_language="Chinese", # English for English text output_path="outputs/seed.wav", ) ``` ### Supported Tasks Each call selects one task and accepts the inputs listed below: | Task | Reference audio | Reference text | `target_language` | Controls | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `seed` | one | required | `Chinese` / `English`, required | — | | `multilingual` | one | required | `German` / `Spanish` / `French` / `Korean` / `Japanese` | — | | `paralinguistic` | one | required | `Chinese` / `English` | inline tags in `text` | | `podcast` | one per speaker | one per speaker, same order | inferred from the text | `speaker_N:` at the start of every line | | `basic` | one | not accepted | — | `speed`, `pitch`, `volume`, all three | | `emotion` | one | not accepted | — | `emotion` | | `dialect` | one | not accepted | — | `dialect`: `川渝话` / `广粤话` | | `freeform` | one | not accepted | — | `instruction` | | `voice_design` | none | — | — | `style` | | `ip` | none | — | — | `ip` | Freeform always requires a reference clip and cannot be combined with voice design, a built-in voice, emotion, dialect or attribute controls. For `podcast`, start every dialogue line with `speaker_N:` and provide one reference audio clip and transcript per speaker, in speaker order. Repeat `--prompt_wav` and `--prompt_text` on the command line. See the [Tiny examples](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts#ming-30-tts-tiny) for a Podcast Python example and [examples/one_click/](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts/tree/main/examples/one_click) for scripts for every task. `python infer_tiny.py --help` lists the CLI arguments. ### Verify the Checkpoint ```bash python tools/preflight_tiny.py --model_path /path/to/Ming-3.0-tts-tiny ``` ## Performance Benchmark comparisons from the [project README](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts#performance). **Bold** and underline mark the best and second-best values among the listed open-source models; ties share a mark. # Ming-3.0-tts-0.5B MLX (8bit)

This is [inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts-0.5B](https://huggingface.co/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts-0.5B) converted for [mlx-audio](https://github.com/Blaizzy/mlx-audio) with `mlx_audio.convert`. The weights are 8-bit affine quantization (group size 64), including the audio VAE; on identical latents the 8-bit VAE decodes at 31 dB SNR against bf16.

Ming-3.0-tts-0.5B is a dense, Qwen2.5-0.5B-based speech model from inclusionAI. It supports:
- zero-shot voice cloning;
- built-in voices;
- freeform and voice-design instructions;
- emotion, speed, pitch and volume control;
- 14 inline paralinguistic tags;
- Chinese, English, German, Spanish, French, Korean and Japanese, plus Sichuanese and Cantonese.

It outputs 44.1 kHz audio. See the [original model card](https://huggingface.co/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts-0.5B) and the [Ming-3.0-tts repository](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-tts) for details.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Size on disk | 1.5 GB |
| Real-time factor (M4 Pro) | 0.39 |
| Peak memory | 2.2 GB |

## Install

Ming-3.0 needs the prompt-contract fix in [mlx-audio #1047](https://github.com/Blaizzy/mlx-audio/pull/1047). With an mlx-audio release that predates it, the model loads but says the wrong words. Until it is released, install from that branch (or from `main` once it merges):

```bash
pip install "git+https://github.com/cguldogan/mlx-audio.git@ming3-dense"
```

## Use

```bash
# Text to speech
mlx_audio.tts.generate --model mlx-community/Ming-3.0-tts-0.5B-8bit \
  --text "The evening wind blew in from the mountain pass, and the distant clouds slowly turned gold."

# Voice cloning: pass the reference clip and its exact transcript
mlx_audio.tts.generate --model mlx-community/Ming-3.0-tts-0.5B-8bit \
  --text "I never thought a little machine could sound this much like me." \
  --ref_audio reference.wav --ref_text "Exact transcript of reference.wav."

# Built-in voice
mlx_audio.tts.generate --model mlx-community/Ming-3.0-tts-0.5B-8bit \
  --text "Good evening, and welcome to the late news." --voice UK_Charlotte

# Freeform instruction
mlx_audio.tts.generate --model mlx-community/Ming-3.0-tts-0.5B-8bit \
  --text "The old radio crackled softly as the storm moved across the valley." \
  --instruct "Speak in a warm, intimate storytelling voice, with a gentle pace and a hint of nostalgia." \
  --use_zero_spk_emb

# German, Spanish, French, Korean or Japanese
mlx_audio.tts.generate --model mlx-community/Ming-3.0-tts-0.5B-8bit \
  --text "Am Wochenende haben wir im kleinen Café am Bahnhof einen Kuchen gegessen." --lang_code de
```

```python
from mlx_audio.tts.models.bailingmm.bailingmm import ming3_instruction
from mlx_audio.tts.utils import load_model

model = load_model("mlx-community/Ming-3.0-tts-0.5B-8bit")
result = next(model.generate(
    text="[Sigh] The rain still hasn't stopped. [Cough] I guess we'll have to move the party indoors.",
))
happy = next(model.generate(
    text="所有测试都顺利通过了，我们终于可以把这个好消息告诉大家！",
    instruct=ming3_instruction(emotion="高兴"),
    ref_audio="reference.wav",
    ref_text="Exact transcript of reference.wav.",
))
```

More examples, including the full list of tags and control values, are in the [mlx-audio Ming dense README](https://github.com/cguldogan/mlx-audio/blob/ming3-dense/mlx_audio/tts/models/dense/README.md).

## Checks

Each clip was transcribed with whisper-large-v3-turbo. Across English, Chinese, paralinguistic tags, Chinese and English cloning, freeform, German and a 30-second three-fragment paragraph, with three seeds each, 24 of 24 clips were correct.

## Limitations

- **Speaker embeddings.** The CAM++ speaker embedding the reference uses for cloning and for the emotion, attribute and dialect tasks is not extracted yet. Cloning works from the reference audio and transcript alone.
- **Text normalization.** The reference's text normalization is not ported, so write numbers out as words.
- **Stopping.** The stop head occasionally fails to fire, leaving trailing low noise. Re-run with another seed if that happens.

# 𓋹 VoiceTut-TTS **An Open-Source Text-to-Speech Model for Egyptian Arabic & Code-Switching** [![🤗 Model](https://img.shields.io/badge/🤗%20HuggingFace-Model-yellow)](https://huggingface.co/mohammedaly22/VoiceTut-TTS) [![🤗 Space](https://img.shields.io/badge/🤗%20Space-Demo-blue)](https://huggingface.co/spaces/mohammedaly22/VoiceTut-TTS) [![🎧 Samples](https://img.shields.io/badge/🎧%20Audio-Demos-ff9800)](https://mohammedaly22.github.io/VoiceTuT-TTS/) [![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/voicetut-tts?color=blue&label=PyPI)](https://pypi.org/project/voicetut-tts/) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Repo-181717?logo=github)](https://github.com/MohammedAly22/VoiceTuT-TTS) [![Base](https://img.shields.io/badge/Base-OmniVoice-purple)](https://github.com/k2-fsa/OmniVoice) [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache%202.0-green.svg)](https://github.com/MohammedAly22/VoiceTuT-TTS/blob/main/LICENSE) VoiceTut-TTS is an Egyptian-Arabic text-to-speech model fine-tuned from [OmniVoice](https://github.com/k2-fsa/OmniVoice). It produces natural Egyptian speech with seamless **Arabic ↔ English code-switching**, ships **19 built-in voices**, supports **zero-shot voice cloning**, and includes a robust Egyptian-Arabic **text normalization** pipeline plus **true streaming** for long text.
> **Why "VoiceTut"?** *Tut* — after the boy-king **Tutankhamun** (توت عنخ آمون) — anchors the model in Egyptian identity, just as our companion ASR model **[QwenCleo-ASR](https://github.com/MohammedAly22/qwencleo-asr)** is named after **Cleopatra**. Together they form an Egyptian speech stack: **Cleo listens, Tut speaks.** 🎙️🗣️ ## 🔗 Links - 🎧 **Audio demo (VoiceTut vs. base OmniVoice):** https://mohammedaly22.github.io/VoiceTuT-TTS/ - 🚀 **Interactive Space:** https://huggingface.co/spaces/mohammedaly22/VoiceTut-TTS - 💻 **GitHub (code, notebooks):** https://github.com/MohammedAly22/VoiceTuT-TTS - 📦 **PyPI:** https://pypi.org/project/voicetut-tts/ ## ✨ Features - 🎯 **Egyptian-first** — fine-tuned specifically on Egyptian Arabic, not generic MSA. - 🔀 **Code-switching** — handles real Arabic + English mixed speech (`عندي meeting بكرة`). - 🗣️ **19 built-in voices** — male & female speakers. - 🧬 **Zero-shot cloning** — clone any voice from a few seconds of reference audio. - 🔢 **Robust normalization** — numbers, dates, times, currencies, phones, emails, URLs, abbreviations + an English→Arabic name map. - ⚡ **True streaming** — long text is split into sentences and yielded as audio chunks. ## 📦 Installation ```bash # PyTorch matching your CUDA (see https://pytorch.org) pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu121 # OmniVoice backbone (not on PyPI — install from GitHub) pip install git+https://github.com/k2-fsa/OmniVoice.git pip install voicetut-tts ``` ## 🚀 Usage ```python from voicetut_tts import VoiceTutTTS tts = VoiceTutTTS.from_pretrained("mohammedaly22/VoiceTut-TTS") # 1) Built-in speaker tts.synthesize("ازيك عامل ايه النهاردة؟", speaker="Mohammed", output="out.wav") # 2) Zero-shot voice cloning tts.synthesize("النهارده الجو حلو اوي", ref_audio="my_voice.wav", ref_text="ده الصوت بتاعي", output="clone.wav") # 3) Code-switching + generation params tts.synthesize("عندي meeting الساعة 3:30 ومعايا ال presentation", speaker="Yasmin", num_step=48, guidance_scale=2.5, speed=1.05, output="cs.wav") ``` Streaming long text: ```python for sr, chunk in tts.stream(long_paragraph, speaker="Ahmed"): play(chunk) # plays each sentence as it's generated tts.synthesize_long(long_paragraph, "long.wav", speaker="Ahmed") ``` ## 🗣️ Built-in Voices | | Male | Female | |---|---|---| | Names | Ahmed, Ali, Hassan, Karim, Mahmoud, Mohammed, Mostafa, Ramy, Shaker, Tareq, Yehia, Youssef | Hadeer, Hanan, Mariam, Rana, Sarah, Yasmin, Yara | Each voice ships with a reference clip. Browse and listen in the [Space](https://huggingface.co/spaces/mohammedaly22/VoiceTut-TTS). ## 📊 Performance > Measured on a single **NVIDIA T4 (Colab)**, `float16`, `num_step=32`. Reproduce with [`examples/04_evaluation.ipynb`](https://github.com/MohammedAly22/VoiceTuT-TTS/blob/main/examples/04_evaluation.ipynb). | Metric | Value | |---|---| | Real-time factor (RTF, mean) | **1.13×** | | RTF (best) | **0.49×** | | Time-to-first-audio (streaming) | **1.68 s** | | Peak VRAM (fp16) | **2.93 GB** | | WER — Egyptian Arabic | **0.40** | | WER — English | **0.07** | | Speaker similarity (cloning, cosine) | **0.83** | | Naturalness (UTMOS, 1–5) | **3.47** | | Sampling rate | 24 kHz | > On A100 / H100 expect markedly lower RTF and TTFA. ## 🏗️ Model - **Base model:** [k2-fsa/OmniVoice](https://github.com/k2-fsa/OmniVoice) (Qwen3-0.6B text backbone + Higgs audio tokenizer) - **Language id:** `arz` (Egyptian Arabic), with English code-switching (`en`) ## ⚠️ Responsible Use Voice cloning is provided to enable **beneficial** use cases — voice assistants, accessibility, educational and creative content. **Do not** use it to impersonate real people, produce deceptive or misleading audio, or harm, harass, or defraud anyone. Always obtain consent before cloning a real person's voice, and disclose synthetic audio where appropriate. ## 📜 License & Citation Apache-2.0. ```bibtex @software{voicetut_tts_2026, author = {Mohammed Aly}, title = {VoiceTut-TTS: Egyptian Arabic & Code-Switching Text-to-Speech}, year = {2026}, url = {https://github.com/MohammedAly22/VoiceTuT-TTS}, note = {Fine-tuned from OmniVoice} } ```

# mimetic-a0

A text-to-audio model for music, trained only on audio with a clean licence: Freesound clips released as CC0, and synthetic music rendered by our own procedural generators. It writes 48 kHz stereo, up to 16 s: drum loops, basslines, chords, melodies, pads, one-shots and full mixes, at the tempo, key and chords you ask for.

**Speed.** A 12 s clip at 50 steps takes:

| | fp32 (`model.safetensors`, 2.0 GB) | fp16 (`model.fp16.safetensors`, 1.0 GB) |
|---|---|---|
| NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 | 1.7 s | 0.4 s |
| Apple M1 Max (32 GB) | 6.7 s | 6.7 s |

The fp16 version (`--half`) needs about half the memory: generating a 12 s clip on the M1 Max peaked at 2.2 GB in fp16 against 4.1 GB in fp32. It is four times faster on an NVIDIA GPU, whose tensor cores do fp16 arithmetic at several times the fp32 rate. On the M1 Max it runs at the same speed as fp32 and only saves memory: its GPU does fp16 matrix multiplication at the same rate as fp32 (we measured 7.1 and 6.6 TFLOPS), and the diffusion transformer's time is mostly matrix multiplication. Loading the model adds about 10 s to each command-line run; the web UI loads it once.

**A base for fine-tuning.** mimetic-a0 is also intended as a base model for fine-tuning, and we will be releasing updates for this.

Version 0.1, an early release. Internally it is cc0-sampler v4, checkpoint "anneal 120k".

**Run it:** [github.com/micknoise/mimetic-a0](https://github.com/micknoise/mimetic-a0) has a command-line tool and a local web UI (generate, retake, repaint) for NVIDIA GPUs, Apple Silicon Macs and the CPU.

## Usage

With the [mimetic-a0](https://github.com/micknoise/mimetic-a0) package:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/micknoise/mimetic-a0 && cd mimetic-a0 && uv sync
uv run mimetic-a0-webui                     # http://127.0.0.1:8799
uv run mimetic-a0 "finger bass bassline, over Cm - Fm - G7" --bpm 95 --bars 4 -n 4
```

With stock [stable-audio-tools](https://github.com/Stability-AI/stable-audio-tools) (commit `3241adb` or later):

```python
import torch, torchaudio
from stable_audio_tools import get_pretrained_model
from stable_audio_tools.inference.generation import generate_diffusion_cond

model, config = get_pretrained_model("micknoisemachine/mimetic-a0")
model = model.to("cuda").eval()             # or "mps" on Apple Silicon
bpm, bars = 90, 4
seconds = bars * 240 / bpm
audio = generate_diffusion_cond(
    model, steps=50, cfg_scale=6, sample_size=config["sample_size"], seed=1, device="cuda",
    conditioning=[{"prompt": "boom bap drum loop, standard kit, swung, 90 BPM, 4 bars",
                   "seconds_start": 0, "seconds_total": seconds}],
)
audio = audio[0, :, : int(seconds * 48000)].float().cpu()
torchaudio.save("out.wav", audio / audio.abs().max() * 0.9, 48000)
```

It does not load in ComfyUI's Stable Audio nodes, which expect Stable Audio Open's autoencoder.

## Prompting

The model learned almost everything it knows from captions written by its own data generators, so it follows that wording best. **[PROMPTING.md](https://huggingface.co/micknoisemachine/mimetic-a0/blob/main/PROMPTING.md)** lists every instrument, style and clause it knows, with tested examples. In short, a prompt is what it is, then the music, then tempo, key and length, and the duration should match the bars (seconds = bars × 240 ÷ BPM):

```
hip hop drum loop, standard kit, swung, with ghost notes, 90 BPM, 4 bars
electric piano chords, chords Am7 - D9 - Gmaj7, smooth, sustained, 100 BPM, G major, 2 bars
grand piano chord, Cmaj7/E, rolled, first inversion, soft
single cello note, G3
```

## Model

- A 326M-parameter diffusion transformer (1024 wide, 16 layers, 16 heads), rectified flow, in the latent space of the **ACE-Step 1.5 VAE** (MIT; Oobleck architecture, 48 kHz stereo, 64 channels at 25 Hz), which was used frozen as a codec. 511M parameters in all.
- Conditioned on a frozen **T5-base** text encoder (128 tokens) and on `seconds_start` / `seconds_total`, with padding masks for clips shorter than the 16 s window.
- Trained from scratch with stock stable-audio-tools on 2× RTX PRO 6000: batch 256, learning rate 1e-4 (InverseLR) to step 100k, then annealed linearly from 4e-5 to 4e-6 over 20k steps (this checkpoint is the end of that anneal).

## Training data

- **Freesound, CC0 only (35% of draws).** About 276k clips (up to 30 s each), after a provenance review that excluded 2,762 clips on clear evidence: generative-AI outputs and voice clones; commercial packs, Apple Loops, game, film and YouTube rips; two broadcast sound-effects libraries; named Amen breaks. Prompts are rebuilt from each clip's title, tags and description.
- **Synthetic music (65%).** 1.53M items rendered by our own procedural generators: beats in 17 styles, drum one-shots, chords from triads to 13ths, single notes and phrases for each instrument, loops, electronic tracks and band and orchestral pieces. Each item is cut into bar-aligned windows of 1, 2 or 4 bars, each with a caption computed from the notes actually played there: instruments heard, chords in order, density, swing, articulation, dynamics, tempo, key and length. Most instruments are rendered through the **GeneralUser GS** SoundFont (v2.0.3, S. Christian Collins), dry; a synth engine renders the rest, keeping its reverb and delay.

**About the GeneralUser GS SoundFont:** its author allows its use "without restriction for your own music creation, private or commercial". Its author also notes that the origin of some of its samples is uncertain, though none came from commercial packs. Most of the synthetic data rests on it.

**About the CC0 tags:** a CC0 tag is the uploader's claim. The review screened for song-like material (with CLAP and AcoustID fingerprints, which found no named commercial recordings) and for stated sources, but an unlabelled clip could still slip through.

## Evaluation

The checks below compare the base checkpoint at 100k, where the anneal started, with our earlier model (cc0-sampler v2, 200k steps). They use held-out generator seeds for ground truth (tempo, pitch, chords, instruments) and 44 earlier prompts × 4 seeds for CLAP prompt match. The anneal (105k–120k) stayed within noise of 100k on every measure, with slightly cleaner takes.

| | mimetic-a0 base (100k) | cc0-sampler v2 |
|---|---|---|
| Tempo on beat prompts | 209/272 | 210/272 |
| Held-out tempo | 83% | 67% |
| Tempo from the BPM in the text | 88% | 68% |
| Pitch of single notes | 94% | 84% |
| Chords | 77% | 18% |
| Instrument identification | 41% | 38% |
| CLAP prompt match: beats / synth parts / instruments | 0.399 / 0.267 / 0.194 | 0.388 / 0.275 / 0.244 |

CLAP scores the GeneralUser GS instruments below real recordings, which pulls its instrument score down.

## Intended use and limits

For making samples and parts for music: loops, one-shots, basslines, chords, melodies and sketches of full mixes.

- **Music first.** SFX, foley and field recordings are weak.
- **Wording.** It follows the vocabulary in PROMPTING.md best; far-off phrasings ("120bpm", "strumming") follow less reliably.
- **Timbre.** Most instruments sound like General MIDI samples, dry.
- **4/4 only**, 1, 2 or 4 bars, at most 16 s.
- **The autoencoder** sets a ceiling on quality: upper harmonics are 16 dB down at 15–20 kHz, there is some aliasing above 5 kHz, clicks come out softer, and noise textures can be up to 10 dB off.
- **Tempo** on fast, busy beats (trap, drum and bass) is less reliable; take several variations.
